_about: Hand-curated 2026-11-14. Each cell: what the drug does to a signal a wearable reads, what that means for a heat alert, and the evidence behind it. level: heat = measured in people in heat; lab = controlled heat/exercise study, usually healthy young volunteers; pharm = known pharmacology, not tested in heat; none = nothing found. effect: blunts | raises | suppresses | lowers | confounds | useful

Heart rate.text: Propranolol blunted the heart-rate rise in heat. HR-based strain alerts and HR-derived core-temperature estimates will under-read strain.

Skin temperature.text: Less skin blood flow during exercise in heat; skin stays cooler while core heat builds.

Sweat / EDA.text: Studies disagree: less sweat at a given core temperature in one, transiently more with propranolol in others.

Core temperature.text: Heat tolerance unchanged in one study, but propranolol raised fluid needs; core measurement is the safer signal.

Weight / hydration.text: Non-selective beta blockade increased fluid needs during prolonged exercise.

Heart rate.text: Atropine raised heart rate in heat; HR alerts may fire early or from a shifted baseline.

Skin temperature.text: Atropine both suppresses sweat and widens skin vessels; skin temperature rose in hot-dry conditions. Skin-temperature cooling models do not hold.

Sweat / EDA.text: Sweating is inhibited. An electrodermal or sweat sensor stays flat even as heat strain builds.

Core temperature.text: Clinical doses did not raise core temperature at rest after exercise, but shortened tolerance in hot-dry heat.

Heart rate.text: Lower plasma volume raises heart rate and noradrenaline during exercise.

Core temperature.text: Diuretic-induced dehydration reduced heat tolerance; some volunteers developed heat exhaustion.

Weight / hydration.text: The drug itself lowers body weight. UKHSA suggests weight to track fluid intake; on a diuretic, daily weight cannot separate the drug's effect from heat dehydration without a baseline.
Starting with a diuretic raised dehydration admissions 2.79-fold; hydration tracking matters most here, but no wearable study exists.

Heart rate.text: Dihydropyridines (nifedipine) can raise HR; verapamil and diltiazem lower it. Direction depends on the agent; not tested in heat.

Core temperature.text: Patients on antipsychotics showed a hyperthermic response to a heat tolerance test. Core temperature is the signal that matters.

Sweat / EDA.text: Agents with anticholinergic load (clozapine, olanzapine) reduce sweating; not measured with a wearable.

Heart rate.text: Clozapine commonly causes resting tachycardia, shifting the HR baseline.

Sweat / EDA.text: SSRIs/SNRIs often increase sweating; tricyclics reduce it. Opposite errors for a sweat sensor.

Core temperature.text: Serotonin syndrome causes hyperthermia unrelated to ambient heat; a core-temperature alert cannot tell the two apart.
A dopamine reuptake inhibitor in heat raised core temperature without changing perceived effort or thermal stress. Symptom-based warnings fail; objective core temperature helps.

Heart rate.text: Raised resting heart rate shifts the HR baseline.

Glucose (CGM).text: The one medicated-wearable pairing studied in heat. Heat raises serious hypoglycaemia; a 2023 heat wave stressed closed-loop pump performance (CGM data).

Skin temperature.text: Warm skin at the injection or infusion site speeds insulin absorption (27% higher peak). Site temperature, not body temperature, drives the dose.

Sweat / EDA.text: Reduced sweating (oligohidrosis), mostly in children; pilot study of the adverse effect.

Core temperature.text: Labels warn of hyperthermia and heat stroke with reduced sweating; no wearable study.
